a: master in its own right over the passions
p: Each new proof ends with the sentence the speech set out to prove in 1:1.
b: This is the book's thesis in its own words: godly reason is autodespotos, "master in its own right", over the passions (see 1:1 and 1:7). The speaker states it again after each proof: after Eleazar (6:31-35), after the brothers here, after the mother (16:1), and in the closing appeal (18:2). The verse opens with "if" (ei de toinyn): if the brothers did this, the thesis is proved. The repetition is deliberate. The speech works like a philosopher's demonstration, and each example adds a harder case: an old man, then young men who love one another, then a mother who loves her sons.
orig: αὐτοδέσποτός ἐστιν τῶν παθῶν ὁ εὐσεβὴς λογισμός (autodespotos estin ton pathon ho eusebes logismos)

a: eaten the defiling food
p: The one Greek verb means 'eat defiling food': the pork and idol meat of 5:2.
b: Emierophagesan is one verb, "they ate defiling food" (Swete's copy spells the word miero- for miaro-). The food is what Antiochus ordered in 5:2: pork and meat offered to idols. Eating it was not only breaking a food law: in this setting it meant giving in to the king's demand to abandon the law in public. The brothers' refusal is the proof the speaker needs: if passion had won, they would have eaten.
orig: ἐμιεροφάγησαν (emierophagesan)

a: Think of the towers that jut out at a harbor's mouth.
p: Seven brothers, seven towers: their reasoning is a breakwater that keeps the waters of godliness calm.
b: Ancient harbors were protected by moles, long walls of stone running out into the sea, often with towers at their ends. Inside, ships could anchor in still water. The speaker turns the brothers into "seven towers" (13:7, one Greek word, heptapyrgos) and godliness into the harbor. The passions are the storm outside. The picture comes back when the mother is compared to Noah's ark in the flood (15:31-32). The point is not that the storm stops, but that it cannot get in.
orig: ἡ ἑπτάπυργος τῶν νεανίσκων εὐλογιστία (he heptapyrgos ton neaniskon eulogistia)

a: a holy chorus of godliness
p: A Greek chorus sang and danced together. The brothers move as one, like a chorus.
b: Choros was a group of singers and dancers who performed together at festivals and in plays. The speaker uses the picture three times: the brothers form a holy chorus (13:8), they "danced in a ring around the number seven" (14:8), and in one manuscript of 18:23 they join "the chorus of their fathers" (see the variant there). For readers who lived among Greek festivals, the image turns a torture scene into a sacred performance. Townshend (1913) argued that such openness to Greek images suits a Jewish writer in a Greek city.
orig: ἱερὸν γὰρ εὐσεβείας στήσαντες χορὸν (hieron gar eusebeias stesantes choron)

a: the three young men
p: Hananiah, Azariah and Mishael refused to worship the king's statue and were thrown into fire (Daniel 3).
b: The brothers take as their model the three friends of Daniel who would not bow to Nebuchadnezzar's statue: "And if he does not, O king, let this be known to you: we do not serve your gods" (Daniel 3:18). The comparison fits closely: a king, a public test of loyalty, and fire. But the three were rescued from the furnace, and the brothers will not be. The book uses the three again in 16:3, 16:21 and 18:12, and 1 Maccabees 2:59 names them among the faithful. Daniel sets the story "in the province of Babylon" (Daniel 3:1); on "Syria", see the variant.

a: Hold out like a nobleman!
p: Eugenos means 'as the well-born do'. The brothers speak like noblemen, though Antiochus treats them as slaves.
b: Eugenos comes from eugenes, "well-born, noble". In the Greek world, nobility meant both birth and the courage expected of the high-born. The book uses this word family often for its martyrs (the "noble mother", 15:24; the contest is "noble", 16:16). The brothers are sons of Abraham, and that is their nobility. The verb is karterēson, "hold out", the book's word for steadfastness.
orig: Εὐγενῶς καρτέρησον (Eugenos karterēson)

a: by whose fatherly hand Isaac was willing to be slaughtered
t: Compared with the Bible: a willing Isaac
p: Genesis does not say Isaac agreed to be sacrificed. 4 Maccabees, like later Jewish tradition, makes him willing.
b: Goes beyond. Genesis tells only what Abraham did: "He bound his son Isaac and put him on the altar, on top of the wood" (Genesis 22:9). The Greek here says Isaac hypemeinen, "endured" or "was willing", to be slaughtered for godliness. That makes Isaac the first martyr, a model for sons who offer themselves. The same idea grew in later Jewish retellings of the binding of Isaac (the Akedah) and in Christian readings that see Isaac as a picture of Christ (Hebrews 11:17-19). Judith reminds its readers "how he tested Isaac" (Judith 8:26). The book returns to Isaac in 16:20 and 18:11.

a: We will give ourselves to God with our whole heart
p: The brothers 'dedicate' themselves to God and lend their bodies to the law. Paul uses similar offering language.
b: Aphierosomen is a word for dedicating a gift to a god, as an offering is set apart in a temple. The brothers give God their souls, which he gave them, and they "lend" (chresomen) their bodies to keep the law. Paul uses a different word but the same picture: "place your bodies before him as a sacrifice that is alive, holy and welcome to God" (Romans 12:1). For Paul the offered body lives on in service; for the brothers it is given up in death. There is no sign that Paul knew this book: both draw on the language of the temple.
orig: τῷ θεῷ ἀφιερώσομεν ἐξ ὅλης τῆς καρδίας (to theo aphierosomen ex holes tes kardias)

a: Let us not fear the man who thinks he will kill us.
p: Jesus told his disciples not to fear those who kill only the body. The brothers say something very like it.
b: Jesus said: "do not fear the people who kill the body but have no power to kill the soul. Instead, fear the One who can destroy soul and body alike in Gehenna" (Matthew 10:28; compare Luke 12:4). The brothers' words have the same shape: do not fear the killer (13:14), because the real danger is to the soul (13:15). Both sayings rest on the belief that a person is more than the body. The likeness shows a shared Jewish way of speaking about martyrdom. 4 Maccabees is usually dated somewhere between about AD 20 and 130, so it is not known which was written first, and the texts do not show that either borrowed from the other.
orig: μὴ φοβηθῶμεν τὸν δοκοῦντα ἀποκτενεῖν (me phobethomen ton dokounta apoktenein)

a: eternal torment is waiting for those who break God's commandment
t: Compared with the Bible: eternal torment
p: The brothers expect eternal punishment for those who betray God's law, as later the New Testament warns.
b: Agrees in part. The Hebrew Bible says little about punishment after death; Daniel 12:2 speaks of some who rise "to shame, to a horror without end". 4 Maccabees speaks plainly of "eternal torment" (aionios basanos) for traitors, and promises the tyrant the same (9:9; 12:12); 18:5 says that he is still punished after death. The New Testament also speaks of eternal punishment (Matthew 25:46). The book gives the threat as a reason for courage: the tortures of a king end, but God's do not. The same word, basanos, is used for both, a deliberate contrast. Christians differ on what eternal punishment means; see the topic page.
orig: κίνδυνος ἐν αἰωνίῳ βασάνῳ κείμενος (kindynos en aionio basano keimenos)

a: we will be received by Abraham, Isaac and Jacob
p: The patriarchs welcome the martyrs after death, as Abraham receives Lazarus in Jesus' parable.
b: The brothers expect to be received at once by Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. In Jesus' parable the poor man dies "and he was carried off by the angels to Abraham's embrace" (Luke 16:22), and Jesus says many "will come from the sunrise and the sunset and lie down to eat with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven" (Matthew 8:11). 4 Maccabees returns to the picture at the end: the sons are "gathered together in the place of their fathers" (18:23). In this book the welcome comes right after death, not at a future resurrection (see the chapter 18 page).

a: God's providence
p: Pronoia, 'forethought', was the philosophers' word for God's care of the world.
b: Pronoia means forethought, planning ahead. Greek philosophers, the Stoics most of all, used it for the divine reason that orders the world. Jewish writers in Greek took it over for the God of Israel (Wisdom of Solomon 14:3; 17:2). Here providence is "wise in all things" and has planted family love in every human being. The same providence saves Israel through the martyrs' death in 17:22. Love for one's family is not a weakness to be removed but a gift of God, which makes the brothers' choice harder and their victory greater.
orig: ἡ θεία καὶ πάνσοφος πρόνοια (he theia kai pansophos pronoia)
r: Wisdom of Solomon 14:3; Wisdom of Solomon 17:2; 17:22; 9:24

a: Brotherly love
p: The New Testament uses the same word for love among believers.
b: Philadelphia, "love of brothers", is the word the New Testament uses for the love that members of the church owe one another as a family (Romans 12:10; 1 Thessalonians 4:9; Hebrews 13:1; 1 Peter 1:22). Here it is love between blood brothers, and the speaker explains it almost like a natural scientist: the same womb, the same blood, the same milk, the same schooling in God's law (13:19-22). The surprise of the passage is that this strong love did not hold any brother back from death; it pushed them forward (14:1).
orig: τῆς φιλαδελφίας (tes philadelphias)

a: Even so, the ones left behind held out
p: The book does not ask the brothers to stop loving. Reason rules their love, it does not uproot it.
b: Here the book differs from the strict Stoics. For the Stoics "the virtuous agent feels no passions" and the happy life is "entirely passion-free" (as the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy summarizes them). 4 Maccabees says the reverse earlier: reason is not the uprooter of the passions but their opponent (3:2-5). So the brothers keep their love for one another, which the speaker praises at length, and still hold out. Their reason masters love; it does not kill it. Readers in the Greek lens see the book bending philosophy to the law of Moses, which commands love of family.

a: more kingly than a king, freer than free men
p: The tortured are the true kings and the free, and the king on the throne is the slave of his passions.
b: The paradox runs through the book. Antiochus has power but is driven by passion and rage (8:2; 9:10; 18:20); the brothers are prisoners but rule themselves. Their reasoning is "more royal than a king" because it rules what the king cannot rule: his own passions. Their freedom is not freedom from the law but freedom to obey God's law against a king's command, as the apostles said they must obey God rather than people (Acts 5:29). Jesus speaks of a freedom that comes from the truth (John 8:32-36).

a: as if they were running on the road to immortality
p: The brothers race toward death as a runner toward the finish line, the picture of Hebrews 12:1.
b: The athletic picture begins here and fills chapter 17 (17:11-16). Death is a racecourse whose finish is athanasia, "immortality". The New Testament uses the same image for the Christian life: "Let us keep running the race that lies ahead of us, and keep at it with endurance" (Hebrews 12:1); "I have run the course to the finish" (2 Timothy 4:7). In 4 Maccabees the prize is the soul's immortal life; in the New Testament it is life with Christ and the resurrection. The image was common in Greek moral speech, so a shared picture does not prove a link between the books.
orig: ὥσπερ ἐπ᾽ ἀθανασίας ὁδὸν τρέχοντες (hosper ep' athanasias hodon trechontes)

a: as if godliness were an immortal soul moving them
p: A hard phrase: godliness is the soul, and the seven brothers are its limbs.
b: The Greek says the brothers agreed together "as by an immortal soul of godliness". The picture: as hands and feet move together because one soul moves them, so seven brothers moved together because one godliness moved them. Brenton (1851) keeps it close: "the immortal soul of religion". Venetus adds a word, "being moved", which makes the sense plainer. The Plain English Translation keeps Swete's text and makes the picture clear with "as if".
orig: ὡς ὑπὸ ψυχῆς ἀθανάτου τῆς εὐσεβείας (hos hypo psyches athanatou tes eusebeias)

a: There were seven days in the making of the world, centered on godliness.
p: The seven brothers circle godliness as the seven days of creation do. The Greek is hard.
b: The number seven links the brothers to creation (Genesis 1:1-2:3) and so to the Sabbath. The Greek of 14:7-8 is hard to follow word by word. Townshend (1913) reports that the German scholar Deissmann moved two words to make it read: the seven days circle around the sacred number seven, and the youths circle in a dance around godliness. Townshend also reports the view of the scholar Grimm, that the seven days of each week were given to recall creation, so seven itself becomes a sign of piety. Either way, the speaker sees the seven deaths as a holy completeness, not a tragedy.
orig: καθάπερ γὰρ ἑπτὰ τῆς κοσμοποιίας ἡμέραι περὶ τὴν εὐσέβειαν (kathaper gar hepta tes kosmopoiias hemerai peri ten eusebeian)

a: Now, we shudder just hearing about what those young men went through.
p: The speaker and his hearers are safe. Scholars use this line to ask when and where the speech was given.
b: The hearers only hear of tortures; they do not face them. Townshend (1913) used this verse to argue against the old claim that Josephus wrote the book: Josephus lived through the fall of Jerusalem and would hardly speak as one who knew suffering only by report. Townshend also argued that the speech assumes a community at peace, which he thought suited Alexandria before the persecution there under the emperor Gaius (Caligula) in AD 38-39. Others place the book later or in Antioch (see the book's opening pages). The verse also shows the speaker's aim: to make safe people feel the cost of faithfulness.

a: Even a woman's mind
p: The argument assumes women are weaker, then uses a woman as its strongest proof.
b: The speaker shares the common ancient view that women are weaker in soul (15:5; 16:5). That is what makes his argument work: if even a woman, an old woman and a mother, could master her passions, reason can master anything (16:1-2). But he ends up praising her above the men: "more courageous in endurance than men", "stronger than a man" (15:30; 16:14). 2 Maccabees 7:21 already says she "stirred her womanly thinking with a manly heart". Modern readers note both sides: the book keeps the ancient view of women, and also lets a woman be its greatest hero.

a: the feeling that comes from deep inside
p: Splanchna, the inner organs, were where ancients felt love and pity, as we say 'the heart'.
b: The Greek is splanchna, the inner parts of the body. Greek speakers felt deep emotion there, as English speakers speak of the heart or the gut. The word comes back for the mother in 15:23 ("her heart") and 15:29 ("the contest of the heart"). The New Testament verb splanchnizomai, "to be moved with pity", comes from the same root, and is used of the father of the lost son (Luke 15:20) and of Jesus (Mark 1:41).
orig: πρὸς τὴν τῶν σπλάγχνων συνπάθειαν (pros ten ton splanchnon synpatheian)

a: Take the birds.
p: Birds defend their young: an old image of a mother's love, used also by Jesus and the law of Moses.
b: The speaker turns to nature to show how strong a mother's love is: birds shield their chicks and circle crying when they cannot. The law of Moses protects a mother bird on her nest (Deuteronomy 22:6-7), and Jesus uses a mother bird for his love for Jerusalem: "the way a bird gathers her young under her wings" (Matthew 23:37). Townshend (1913) reports that Gregory of Nazianzus, preaching on the Maccabees, took over this picture of the mother bird and applied it directly to the mother. The point here is that the mother's love was not smaller than a bird's; it was overruled by something greater.

a: Even bees
p: Ancient writers admired bees as fierce defenders of their hive.
b: Greek and Roman writers on nature often praised bees for their order and their fierce defense of the hive. The Bible uses bees as a picture of an army that will not let go: the Amorites "chased you the way bees do" (Deuteronomy 1:44, see that page). Here the bee is the last and smallest example: even an insect fights to the death for its young. The mother will do something stranger: she will urge her young to die.

a: who had a soul like Abraham's
p: Homopsychos, 'same-souled': she was of one soul with Abraham, who was ready to give up his son.
b: Homopsychos means "of the same soul". The comparison is with Abraham at the binding of Isaac (Genesis 22), when he was ready to give up the son God had promised. The book makes the mother Abraham's true daughter (15:28; 17:6; 18:20) and her sons Abraham's children (18:1, 23). Her test is greater than his in one way: Abraham gave up one son and received him back; she gives up seven. The comparison is the backbone of chapters 14-16.
orig: τὴν Ἀβραὰμ ὁμόψυχον τῶν νεανιῶν μητέρα (ten Abraam homopsychon ton neanion metera)

a: tyrant over the passions
p: The speaker calls reason a tyrant over the passions, a jab at the real tyrant.
b: The Greek calls reason tyrannos, the same word the book uses for Antiochus, "the tyrant". The word play is bold: there are two tyrants in the story. Antiochus rules others by force but cannot rule himself. The sons' reason rules the passions completely, as a tyrant rules his subjects. In the end the true tyrant wins (16:14; 17:2).
orig: Ὦ λογισμὲ τέκνων παθῶν τύραννε (O logisme teknon pathon tyranne)

a: for a short time
p: The choice is between safety for a time and life for ever.
b: Proskairos means "for a season, temporary". The book sets it against "eternal life" (15:3), and repeats it in 15:8, 15:23 and 15:27. Paul uses the same pair of words: "What we see lasts only a while; what we cannot see lasts forever" (2 Corinthians 4:18). The tyrant's promise is real, but short. The mother weighs the two, like a judge or a council (15:25-26), and chooses what lasts.
orig: τῆς ἑπτὰ υἱῶν σωτηρίας προσκαίρου (tes hepta huion soterias proskairou)

a: the godliness that keeps people safe for eternal life with God
p: 4 Maccabees speaks of eternal life, as the New Testament does, but means the soul's life with God.
b: Agrees and differs. "Eternal life" (aionios zoe) is the phrase of Daniel 12:2 in Greek and of the Gospels (John 3:16). Here it is the reward of godliness, kept by obedience to the law until death. In the New Testament eternal life is God's gift through Christ (Romans 6:23) and includes the raising of the body. In 4 Maccabees it is the life of the immortal soul with God (16:13; 17:18; 18:23). The words match; the hope behind them is not the same.
orig: τὴν σώζουσαν εἰς αἰώνιον ζωὴν κατὰ θεόν (ten sozousan eis aionion zoen kata theon)

a: the weaker in spirit mothers are
p: The speaker shares the ancient belief that women are weaker and so feel more. His point is how strong her love was.
b: Asthenopsychos, "weak-souled", is the speaker's word. He reasons that mothers love more because they are weaker and because they bear more children. Modern readers will not share his view of women. But his aim is not to belittle the mother: it is to show how strong the passion was that she mastered. The weaker the soul, by his logic, the greater the victory (14:11).
orig: ἀσθενόψυχοι (asthenopsychoi)

a: They were just, self-restrained and courageous.
p: Three of the four Greek virtues of 1:2-4, plus 'great-souled'.
b: The list repeats three of the four virtues the speech defined at the start: justice, self-restraint (sophrosyne) and courage (1:2-4, 18). The fourth, good sense, is shown by their choice. They are also megalopsychoi, "great-souled". The speaker adds two family virtues, love of brothers and love of mother, and joins them to the law: they obeyed their mother by keeping the law. In this book, the Greek virtues and the law of Moses come out of the same training.
orig: δίκαιοί τε γὰρ ἦσαν καὶ σώφρονες καὶ ἀνδρεῖοι καὶ μεγαλόψυχοι (dikaioi te gar esan kai sophrones kai andreioi kai megalopsychoi)

a: like masks
p: The flayed skin hung like the masks actors wore. The speaker shows the horror without softening it.
b: Prosopeia are theater masks. The image is of the scalp pulled down over the face, a torture already in 2 Maccabees 7:4, 7. The speaker dwells on such scenes on purpose. Townshend (1913) remarks that the first hearers lived where torture was seen in public, and that the detail was meant to show how much the mother overcame. The Plain English Translation gives the scenes plainly, as the Greek does, without adding to them.
orig: ὥσπερ προσωπεῖα προκειμένας (hosper prosopeia prokeimenas)

a: who gave birth to complete godliness
p: She did not only give birth to sons; she brought complete godliness into the world.
b: Holokleros means "complete in every part", whole, with nothing missing. The speaker says she alone "gave birth to" godliness in its wholeness: her seven sons, and her own choice, are godliness lived out to the end. James uses the same word: "so that you may be complete and whole" (James 1:4). The verse is part of a long praise speech addressed straight to the mother (15:16-32).
orig: τὴν εὐσέβειαν ὁλόκληρον ἀποκυήσασα (ten eusebeian holokleron apokyesasa)

a: They stared like a bull's
p: Taurēdon, 'bull-like', is the word Plato used for Socrates' look just before he drank the poison.
b: Tauredon means "in the manner of a bull": a fixed, glaring look from under the brows. It is rare. Plato uses it in the Phaedo (117b) for Socrates, who looked at the jailer "like a bull" as he took the cup of poison. Educated hearers may have caught the echo: the brothers face death with the calm defiance of Greece's most famous martyr for truth. That the writer meant the echo cannot be proved, but he knew Greek literature well.
orig: ταυρηδὸν (tauredon)

a: a mass grave
p: Polyandrion was the common grave of the dead after a battle.
b: Polyandrion, literally "the place of many men", was the word for a common burial ground, especially the grave of soldiers fallen in battle. The torture ground has become a war grave for one family. The Greek of Jeremiah uses the word for the valley of Hinnom, the "common grave of slaughter" (Jeremiah 19:6 in Greek). The heaped flesh and bodies in this verse make the picture literal.
orig: πολυάνδριον (polyandrion)

a: No songs of the Sirens, no swan's voice
p: The speaker borrows two famous Greek images of sounds that pull hearers in.
b: In Homer's Odyssey the Sirens sing so sweetly that sailors steer to their death; Odysseus has himself tied to the mast to hear them. The swan was said to sing its most beautiful song as it died. The speaker says the cries of the dying sons pulled at their mother more than either. Verdict: this is a literary ornament, not a belief. The writer uses Greek myth as an educated speaker would, the way English speakers say "siren song" or "swan song" today, without any sign that he believed in the Sirens.

a: the mother herself was tortured
p: Her sons' tortures were her own. Christian preachers saw in her a picture of Mary at the cross.
b: She is not touched until the end (17:1), but every torture of her sons tortures her. Townshend (1913) reports that Gregory of Nazianzus, in his sermon on the Maccabees, saw in this mother's agony what Townshend calls "a true foretype of the Mother of Sorrows" at the cross, and put in her mouth words such as "blessed shall I be among women". Simeon told Mary, "a sword will run right through your soul" (Luke 2:35). Gregory's reading is a Christian one; the book itself knows nothing of it.

a: gave her heart a man's courage
p: Andreioo, 'make manly', from the word for courage (andreia), which itself comes from the word for 'man'.
b: In Greek, courage is andreia, "manliness". So the verb andreiosas means "made her courageous" and "made her manly" at once. The same thought is in 2 Maccabees 7:21, where she "stirred her womanly thinking with a manly heart". 4 Maccabees goes further and says she outdid men (15:30; 16:14). See the note on 14:11.
orig: ἀνδρειώσας (andreiosas)

a: embraced them and let them go
p: The Greek may mean she embraced her sons and released them, or that she cast off her feelings.
b: The Greek says she aspasasa, "having embraced" or "having welcomed", and then exelysen, "let loose" or "undid". It has no object, so the reader must supply one: her sons, whom she held and then gave up to death, or her feelings, which she let go. Brenton (1851) supplies "her feelings". Swete's apparatus reports that R. L. Bensly proposed anaspasasa, "having pulled up", relying on the Syriac version. The Plain English Translation gives the plain sense of the Greek and leaves the object open.
orig: ἀσπάσασα ἡ γενναία μήτηρ ἐξέλυσεν (aspasasa he gennaia meter exelysen)

a: in the council chamber of her own soul
p: Her soul is a city council: her feelings argue, and she holds the votes.
b: A bouleuterion was the hall where a Greek city's council met. The speaker stages the mother's choice as a vote: nature, birth, love of children and the sight of torture are "fierce counselors" pleading one way. She holds two psephoi, the pebbles Greeks used to vote, one for death and one for life (15:26). The picture fits the book's thesis: reason presides, and the passions only advise. She votes for death, because she remembers Abraham (15:28).
orig: καθάπερ γὰρ ἐν βουλευτηρίῳ τῇ ἑαυτῆς ψυχῇ (kathaper gar en bouleuterio te heautes psyche)

a: as a daughter of Abraham
p: The title Luke's Jesus gives to a bent woman he heals. Here it praises the mother's faith.
b: The mother is called Abraham's daughter, a title of faith and family both: she shares his "God-fearing steadfastness" in giving up a son. Luke's Gospel gives the same title to a woman bent over for eighteen years: "this woman, a daughter of Abraham" (Luke 13:16). In Luke it gives honor to someone overlooked; here it crowns a heroine. Both uses say that Abraham's family includes its women by right. The title returns in 17:6 and 18:20 ("Abraham's daughter").

a: O mother of the nation
p: She is given titles fit for a hero of the state: mother of the nation, defender of the law, prize-winner.
b: Each title is grand. Meter ethnous, "mother of the nation", makes her a mother of all Israel, as Sarah is a mother of nations (Genesis 17:16). Ekdike tou nomou, "defender" or "avenger of the law", is a word for one who wins justice. Hyperaspisteia is one who holds a shield over another; the Plain English Translation says "shield of godliness". Athlophore, "prize-winner", is the athlete's word that returns for her in 18:23. The titles prepare for the athletic contest of chapter 17.
orig: Ὦ μήτηρ ἔθνους, ἔκδικε τοῦ νόμου, καὶ ὑπερασπίστεια τῆς εὐσεβείας (O meter ethnous, ekdike tou nomou, kai hyperaspisteia tes eusebeias)

a: Noah's ark
p: The ark carried the world through the flood; the mother carried godliness through the storm.
b: God told Noah: "Make yourself an ark of gopher wood" (Genesis 6:14), and in it life on earth was carried through the flood. The speaker plays on words: the flood was kosmoplethes, "world-filling", and the ark was kosmophorousa, "world-carrying". The mother, "guardian of the law", is the ark of godliness, and the passions are the flood. 1 Peter 3:20 uses Noah's ark as a picture of salvation in a different way, as a figure of baptism.
orig: ἡ Νῶε κιβωτὸς ἐν τῷ κοσμοπληθεῖ κατακλυσμῷ κοσμοφοροῦσα (he Noe kibotos en to kosmoplethei kataklysmo kosmophorousa)

a: sovereign over the passions
p: Autokrator, 'ruling by its own power'. The proof from the mother ends with the thesis.
b: Autokrator means "one who rules by his own power". Like 13:1, the verse begins with "if": if even a woman, old and a mother, endured this, the thesis stands. The speech uses it beside autodespotos (13:1) and despotes (18:2) for reason's rule. The case is now complete: men (an old priest, seven young brothers) and a woman, old and a mother, have all shown it (16:2).
orig: αὐτοκράτωρ ἐστὶν τῶν παθῶν ὁ εὐσεβὴς λογισμός (autokrator estin ton pathon ho eusebes logismos)

a: The lions around Daniel
p: Two great dangers of the book of Daniel are less fierce than the love that burned in the mother.
b: Daniel was thrown to the lions (Daniel 6:16), and Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah into the furnace (Daniel 3). The book uses their Hebrew names, given in Daniel 1:6; Daniel 1:7 gives their Babylonian names (Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego). The comparison is surprising: the danger here is inside her, her love for her sons, and it is fiercer than lions or fire. Daniel and the three come back in the mother's own words (16:21; 18:12-13).

a: She might have said something like this
t: The lament she did not make
p: A speaker's device: he writes the speech she might have given, to show what she did not do.
b: Ancient speakers sometimes composed a speech a person could have made, to set off what they really did. The book did the same with the brothers (8:16-26, the speech "the cowards" might have made). Here the mother's imagined lament (16:6-11) is a moving picture of what grief says: wasted pregnancies, no grandchildren, no son to bury her. Then the speaker says plainly that she said none of it (16:11-12). The real speech follows in 16:16-23.

a: Seven times ten months
p: The speaker counts a pregnancy as ten months, as the Wisdom of Solomon does. 2 Maccabees 7:27 says nine.
b: Dekamenoi are "ten-month periods". The Wisdom of Solomon counts the same way: "over a time of ten months" (Wisdom of Solomon 7:2). In 2 Maccabees the mother says, "I bore you in my belly nine months. I nursed you three years" (2 Maccabees 7:27). Neither book explains its count.
orig: ἀνόνητοι ἑπτὰ δεκάμηνοι (anonetoi hepta dekamenoi)

a: I will have no son to bury me
p: To be buried by one's children was a great duty and blessing. Tobit asks it of his son.
b: In the Jewish world, as in the Greek, children buried their parents, and to die with no one to do it was a curse. Tobit tells his son, "See that I am buried well" (Tobit 4:3), and asks him to bury his mother beside him (Tobit 4:4). The imagined lament ends at the bottom of grief. The real mother does not say it, because she expects to be with her sons again (16:13).

a: She was bearing the full number of her sons again, this time into immortality.
t: Compared with the Bible: born again into immortality
p: In 2 Maccabees the mother hopes for the resurrection. Here she gives birth to her sons into immortality.
b: Differs from 2 Maccabees and goes beyond the Hebrew Bible. In 2 Maccabees the mother says the Creator "will give you back the breath and the life in his mercy" (2 Maccabees 7:23), and she hopes to "receive you back with your brothers" (2 Maccabees 7:29): a bodily resurrection. 4 Maccabees retells the same story without the resurrection. Here she "gives birth again" (anatiktousa; Venetus has a different verb, see the variant) to her sons into athanasia, immortality. The new birth is the soul's entry into life with God at death (17:18; 18:23). The New Testament speaks of being born again (John 3:3) and of putting on immortality at the resurrection (1 Corinthians 15:53-54), a different picture. See the chapter 18 page.
orig: εἰς ἀθανασίαν ἀνατίκτουσα τὸν τῶν υἱῶν ἀριθμόν (eis athanasian anatiktousa ton ton huion arithmon)

a: soldier of God
p: The old woman is a soldier, and her endurance wins a battle against a king.
b: The speaker mixes two pictures: the soldier and the athlete. As a soldier of God, the mother wins by enduring, not by fighting back. The New Testament uses the same picture of believers: "Suffer hard things along with me, as Christ Jesus' good soldier" (2 Timothy 2:3), and "Dress yourselves in all of God's armor" (Ephesians 6:11). In 13:16 the brothers "put on, as armor, the rule over the passions".
orig: θεοῦ στρατιῶτι (theou stratioti)

a: you stood and watched Eleazar being tortured
p: 4 Maccabees puts the mother and sons at Eleazar's death. 2 Maccabees tells the two stories separately.
b: In 2 Maccabees, Eleazar's death (2 Maccabees 6:18-31) and the death of the mother and her sons (2 Maccabees 7) are two separate stories, with no sign that the family saw Eleazar die. 4 Maccabees joins them: the mother and her sons were arrested and stood by as he was tortured, and she pointed to him as their model (16:17). The book also calls him a priest (5:4; 17:9), where 2 Maccabees calls him a scribe. The retelling makes one story out of the nine deaths.

a: in the Hebrew language
p: As in 2 Maccabees 7, the mother speaks to her sons in their own tongue. The book does not say why.
b: Te Hebraidi phone, "in the Hebrew tongue". 2 Maccabees says she spoke "in their fathers' tongue" (2 Maccabees 7:21, 27). The language may be Hebrew or Aramaic, the everyday language of Jews in the east; the New Testament also uses "Hebrew" where Aramaic is likely (Acts 21:40). Neither book says why she used it. In 2 Maccabees 7:27 she speaks this way in front of the king himself.
orig: ἐν τῇ Ἐβραΐδι φωνῇ (en te Hebraidi phone)

a: to testify on behalf of the nation
p: Diamartyria, 'testimony', comes from the same word as 'martyr', which first meant 'witness'.
b: The Greek martys means "witness". In Christian use it came to mean one who bears witness by dying: a martyr. Here the mother calls her sons to diamartyria, solemn testimony, for the nation. Their death is a public witness to what Israel believes. The youngest brother uses the related word martyria when he refuses to desert his brothers' witness (12:17); the idea of the martyr is on its way. The New Testament speaks of Stephen as a witness whose blood was shed (Acts 22:20) and of Antipas, "my faithful witness" (Revelation 2:13).
orig: ὑπὲρ τῆς διαμαρτυρίας τοῦ ἔθνους (hyper tes diamartyrias tou ethnous)

a: the father of our nation
p: Ethnopator, 'nation-father', a rare title for Isaac: through him the nation came.
b: Ethnopator is a rare word. It makes Isaac the father from whom the nation came, and so makes Abraham's test greater: in killing Isaac he would have killed the nation's future. Genesis says Abraham "got up early in the morning" (Genesis 22:3); the speaker turns that into "hurried". The mother's lesson: if Abraham could give up the nation's father for God, she can give up her sons.
orig: τὸν ἐθνοπάτορα υἱὸν (ton ethnopatora huion)

a: he did not cower
p: The Greek does not say whether Abraham or Isaac did not cower at the sword.
b: The grammar lets the subject stay Abraham: he did not flinch at the sight of his own hand bringing down the sword. But the words "coming down on him" suit Isaac, who saw his father's hand above him and did not cower. Brenton (1851) takes it as Abraham. Townshend (1913) takes it as Isaac ("and Isaac, seeing his father's hand lifting the knife against him, did not shrink"), and notes that the Syriac version reads "Isaac, seeing". That fits 13:12, where Isaac is willing. Sinaiticus leaves out "seeing" (Swete's apparatus). The Plain English Translation keeps the Greek's "he" and leaves it open.
orig: τὴν πατρῴαν χεῖρα ξιφηφόρον καταφερομένην ἐπ᾽ αὐτὸν ὁρῶν οὐκ ἔπτηξεν (ten patroan cheira xiphephoron katapheromenen ep' auton horon ouk eptexen)

a: Daniel the righteous was thrown to the lions.
p: Abraham, Daniel and the three in the fire: the same heroes as 1 Maccabees 2 and Hebrews 11.
b: The mother lists the heroes who endured for God, as Mattathias does on his deathbed: "Hananiah, Azariah and Mishael trusted, and they were kept safe from the flame" (1 Maccabees 2:59); "Daniel, for his integrity, was rescued from the lions' mouth" (1 Maccabees 2:60). Hebrews 11 has the same kind of list: those who "shut lions' mouths" (Hebrews 11:33) and "put out the power of fire" (Hebrews 11:34). But those heroes were rescued; the mother's sons will not be. Their "endurance" is the point, not their rescue. A longer list comes in 18:11-13.

a: the same faith in God
p: Pistis here means loyal trust: holding on to God when he does not rescue.
b: Pistis is faith, trust and faithfulness at once. The book uses it rarely, and always for loyalty under pressure: the mother's "faith in God" (15:24), the "nobility of faith" (17:2). Here the sons share the faith of Abraham, Daniel and the three. Hebrews 11 uses the same word for the same kind of heroes, many of them sufferers who "would not take the release they were offered" (Hebrews 11:35). In Hebrews faith looks to God's promise; in this speech, to God himself and to life with him.
orig: τὴν αὐτὴν πίστιν πρὸς τὸν θεὸν ἔχοντες (ten auten pistin pros ton theon echontes)

a: those who die for God's sake live to God
p: Jesus says the same of the patriarchs: 'to him all are alive' (Luke 20:38).
b: The sons know that those who die for God "live to God", like the patriarchs. The book says it also in 7:19. Jesus answers the Sadducees with the same thought about Abraham, Isaac and Jacob: "He is not God of dead people but of living ones, for to him all are alive" (Luke 20:38). Jesus uses it to prove the resurrection; 4 Maccabees means that the patriarchs and martyrs live now with God. Scholars note the shared phrase; whether either text knew the other cannot be shown.
orig: ζῶσιν τῷ θεῷ (zosin to theo)

a: she flung herself onto the pyre
t: Did the mother take her own life?
p: 4 Maccabees says she threw herself into the fire so no one would touch her. Readers have judged this differently.
b: 2 Maccabees says only that the mother died last (2 Maccabees 7:41); 4 Maccabees adds the guards' report that she threw herself on the pyre so that no one would touch her. Readers have judged this differently. Jewish tradition: the Talmud ends its story of the woman and her seven sons, "She too in the end went up to the roof, fell, and died", and honors her as a joyful mother of children (Bavli Gittin 57b, citing Psalm 113:9; translation on Sefaria). Townshend (1913) notes that the Hebrew Bible nowhere forbids the act, that 2 Maccabees praises Razis's self-chosen death (2 Maccabees 14:41-46), and that the nearest biblical case is Saul (1 Samuel 31:4). Christian tradition: Augustine held that killing oneself breaks the commandment against killing, yet would not condemn honored women martyrs who may have acted at God's prompting (City of God 1.20, 1.26). Gregory of Nazianzus, as Townshend reports, praised her for running to the pyre "as to her bride-bed". See also 12:20.

a: showed how noble faith is
p: The mother and her sons broke the tyrant's power by refusing him, not by fighting.
b: The verbs are strong: they "broke" (katalysasa) the tyrant's force and "made void" (akyrosasa, a legal word for cancelling a decree) his plans. Antiochus wanted to end the Jews' way of life (17:9); their deaths showed his decree had no power over them. The speaker calls this the gennaiotes, nobility, of faith (see the note on 16:22).
orig: ἐπιδείξασα τὴν τῆς πίστεως γενναιότητα (epideixasa ten tes pisteos gennaioteta)

a: Like a roof nobly set on the pillar of your sons
p: Her sons are the pillars, she is the roof, and the tortures are an earthquake that cannot bring the house down.
b: The picture is of a building: the sons are the pillar (Swete's text is singular; Sinaiticus and Venetus have "pillars", see the variant), the mother the roof resting on them, and the torture an earthquake. The roof does not tilt (aklinos, "without leaning"). Jesus ends the Sermon on the Mount with a house that stands in the storm because it is built on rock (Matthew 7:24-25). The speaker has already used a harbor (13:6-7) and a ship (15:31-32); now a house.
orig: σὺ στέγη ἐπὶ τοῦ στύλου τῶν παίδων γενναίως ἱδρυμένη (sy stege epi tou stylou ton paidon gennaios hidrymene)

a: The moon does not stand as grand among the stars
p: The mother and her sons now shine in heaven, as Daniel 12:3 promised for the wise.
b: Daniel promised: "Those who put the many in the right will blaze like the stars, for ever and ever" (Daniel 12:3). The speaker places the mother and her sons in heaven like the moon among stars. God had shown Abraham the stars and said, "So will your offspring be" (Genesis 15:5); here the sons of Abraham's daughter become stars. In Daniel the shining follows the resurrection (Daniel 12:2); here it is the place of the souls with God (17:18). Compare the Wisdom of Solomon on the righteous dead: "they will flash out" (Wisdom of Solomon 3:7).
r: Daniel 12:2-3; Genesis 15:5; Matthew 13:43; Wisdom of Solomon 3:7; 17:18

a: like some painter
p: The speaker wishes the scene could be painted. Some scholars see here a Jew at home in a Greek city.
b: The law of Moses forbade images for worship (Exodus 20:4). Yet the speaker wishes, "if it were open to us", that a painter could show the scene. Townshend (1913) took this, with the athletic pictures of 17:11-16, as a sign that the writer lived in a cosmopolitan Greek city where such talk would not shock, and he thought of Alexandria. Swete's text has hosper tinos, "like some (painter)". The first hand of Sinaiticus and Venetus read hos epi tinos, which Townshend translated "as might some artist", taking epi as "in the style of". A scholar's guess, pinakos, "as on a tablet", has no manuscript behind it, as Townshend says. See the variant.
orig: ὥσπερ τινός, ζωγραφῆσαι (hosper tinos, zographesai)

a: on the tomb itself
p: Greeks carved verse epitaphs on tombs. The speaker composes one for the nine martyrs.
b: Greek tombs often carried short inscriptions beginning "Here lies" (entautha). The speaker writes one for his heroes (17:9-10). Townshend (1913) compared the great monument Simon the Maccabee built for his family at Modein, which "is there to this day" (1 Maccabees 13:30), though 1 Maccabees mentions no inscription. Whether the speaker knew a real tomb of the martyrs is unknown: he says it "would be right" to write this, not that it was written. Later Christians in Antioch honored a shrine of the Maccabean martyrs (see the 2 Maccabees 7 page).

a: the Hebrews' way of life
p: Politeia is a people's whole constitution: its laws, customs and citizenship.
b: Politeia means the whole order of a community: its constitution, its laws, its customs, its citizenship. Antiochus did not only want the Jews to eat pork; he wanted to end Israel as a people living under God's law. 2 Maccabees uses the word the same way (2 Maccabees 4:11; 8:17). The book calls the people "the Hebrews", the old name that set them apart from the Greeks. The epitaph names Eleazar "an old priest" (see 5:4).
orig: τὴν Ἐβραίων πολιτίαν καταλῦσαι (ten Hebraion politian katalysai)

a: fixing their eyes on God
p: The same Greek verb as Hebrews 12:2, 'looking to Jesus', in a scene of endurance.
b: The Greek is eis theon aphorontes, "looking away to God". Hebrews uses the same verb in the same kind of setting, right after its list of tortured heroes: "We fix our eyes on Jesus ... he endured a cross" (Hebrews 12:2, aphorontes eis ... Iesoun). Both picture a contestant who looks away from the pain to the one who gives the prize. The match is close, but the verb was common, and no one can show that Hebrews knew this book.
orig: εἰς θεὸν ἀφορῶντες (eis theon aphorontes)

a: Virtue was the judge who gave out the prizes
p: Athlothetein was the work of the official who ran the Greek games and gave the prizes.
b: The athlothetes was the official who set up and judged the games and handed out the prizes. "At that time" (tote), the day of the martyrdoms, Virtue was the judge, endurance is the test, and the prize is aphtharsia, "incorruption", in long-lasting life. Paul uses the same Greek picture: athletes compete "to receive a crown that fades. We do it for one that never fades" (1 Corinthians 9:25). Where 4 Maccabees has incorruption at death, Paul places it at the resurrection: the body "is sown in decay and raised in what cannot decay" (1 Corinthians 15:42).
orig: ἠθλοθέτει γὰρ τότε ἀρετὴ (ethlothetei gar tote arete)
r: 1 Corinthians 9:24-25; 1 Corinthians 15:42; 1 Corinthians 15:53-54; Wisdom of Solomon 2:23; 17:13-16

a: incorruption
p: Aphtharsia: not decaying, the state of what lasts for ever. Kept apart from 'immortality'.
b: Aphtharsia means freedom from decay. The Plain English Translation keeps it apart from athanasia, "immortality" (14:5; 16:13), as it does in the Wisdom of Solomon, which says God created human beings "for incorruption" (Wisdom of Solomon 2:23). Paul uses both words together for the resurrection body: what is perishable must put on incorruption, and what is mortal must put on immortality (1 Corinthians 15:53-54).
orig: τὸ νῖκος ἐν ἀφθαρσίᾳ ἐν ζωῇ πολυχρονίῳ (to nikos en aphtharsia en zoe polychronio)

a: The world and the whole human race looked on.
p: The whole world watches the martyrs' contest, as Paul says the apostles have become a spectacle.
b: The contest has an audience: the tyrant as opponent, and the world as spectators. Paul uses a similar picture of the apostles' suffering: "we have become a spectacle to the world, to angels and to human beings" (1 Corinthians 4:9). Hebrews speaks of "so huge a cloud of witnesses surrounding us" (Hebrews 12:1); there the faithful dead are the crowd watching the race of the living. In 4 Maccabees the crowd is the living world, watching the dying.

a: she crowned her own athletes
p: Winners at the Greek games got a wreath. The New Testament promises martyrs 'the crown of life'.
b: At the Greek games the winner was crowned with a wreath of leaves. Here the fear of God (theosebeia), pictured as a woman, crowns her athletes. The New Testament uses the same picture: "Stay faithful all the way to death, and I will give you the crown of life" (Revelation 2:10); "he will get the crown of life" (James 1:12); "the crown of righteousness" (2 Timothy 4:8). Christian preachers took the picture over: Townshend (1913) notes that John Chrysostom, preaching on the Maccabees, followed this book in comparing the martyrs' struggle to the athletic contests and their crown to the victors'.
orig: θεοσέβεια δὲ ἐνίκα, τοὺς ἑαυτῆς ἀθλητὰς στεφανοῦσα (theosebeia de enika, tous heautes athletas stephanousa)

a: they now stand beside God's throne
t: Compared with the Bible: before God's throne now
p: The martyrs are with God now. Revelation also shows martyrs before the throne before the end.
b: Agrees in part. 4 Maccabees places the martyrs beside God's throne "now" (nyn). Revelation also shows the souls of martyrs with God before the end: "I saw under the altar the souls of those who had been slaughtered because of the word of God" (Revelation 6:9), and those who came out of the great trouble "are before the throne of God" (Revelation 7:15). But in Revelation the story goes on to a resurrection (Revelation 20:4-6); in 4 Maccabees it does not. What the dead know and do before the resurrection is a question the churches answer differently; see the card at Revelation 6 and the topic page.
orig: τῷ θείῳ νῦν παρεστήκασιν θρόνῳ (to theio nyn parestekasin throno)

a: For Moses says
p: The quotation is Deuteronomy 33:3 in the Greek Old Testament, which differs from the Hebrew.
b: The words match the Greek of Deuteronomy 33:3 exactly: kai pantes hoi hegiasmenoi hypo tas cheiras sou, "and all who have been made holy are under your hands" (Swete's Septuagint). The Hebrew is shorter and has "holy ones" with no verb; the Plain English Translation of the Hebrew reads: "all his holy ones are in your hand" (Deuteronomy 33:3). The speaker reads the Greek word "made holy" as a word about the martyrs, who were consecrated by their death (17:20). He quotes Scripture in Greek, as all his hearers did.
orig: Καὶ πάντες οἱ ἡγιασμένοι ὑπὸ τὰς χεῖράς σου (Kai pantes hoi hegiasmenoi hypo tas cheiras sou)

a: made holy for God's sake
p: Hagiazo, 'consecrate': to be set apart for God. Many read 17:20-22 as sacrifice language; Bailey disputes it.
b: Hagiasthentes, "having been made holy", picks up the word of Deuteronomy 33:3 (17:19). To be made holy is to be set apart for God, as priests, offerings and the temple were. Many readers take the verb as preparing the language of sacrifice in 17:22, as if the martyrs were an offering consecrated to God. Daniel Bailey disputes this: he writes that the martyrs are not "compared with victims of sacrifice", and he reads the image of 17:22 as a Greek votive gift (see the chapter page). Hebrews uses the verb of Christ's death: Jesus suffered "so that by his own blood he might make the people holy" (Hebrews 13:12). Sinaiticus leaves out "for God's sake" in its first hand.
orig: ἁγιασθέντες διὰ θεὸν (hagiasthentes dia theon)

a: the homeland was made clean
p: The martyrs' death cleansed the land, which the persecution had defiled.
b: Katharisthenai, "to be cleansed", is the word of purification. Under Antiochus the temple and the land were defiled, and after the victory Judas said, "Now let us go up and make the holy place clean" (1 Maccabees 4:36). 4 Maccabees says the martyrs' death was itself the cleansing. Eleazar prayed for this in his last words: "make my blood their cleansing" (see 6:28-29). The same root is in Leviticus 16:30 in Greek, on the Day of Atonement: "atonement will be made for you, to make you clean".
orig: τὴν πατρίδα καθαρισθῆναι (ten patrida katharisthenai)

a: a life in exchange for the nation's sin
p: Antipsychon means a life given for another life: the martyrs paid with their lives for the nation's sin.
b: Antipsychon is made of anti, "in place of", and psyche, "life, soul": something given in exchange for a life. The word is rare. Eleazar used it in his prayer (see 6:28-29); here it sums up all nine deaths. "As it were" (hosper) softens it: the speaker knows he is using a picture. The idea is that Israel's sin had brought the persecution (as 2 Maccabees 7:18, 32-33 says), and the martyrs' deaths paid what the nation owed. Townshend (1913) and older English versions translate "ransom"; the Plain English Translation keeps the shape of the Greek. Jesus spoke of giving "his life as a ransom in place of many" (Mark 10:45), with different words (lytron anti pollon).
orig: ὥσπερ ἀντίψυχον γεγονότας τῆς τοῦ ἔθνους ἁμαρτίας (hosper antipsychon gegonotas tes tou ethnous hamartias)

a: Through the blood of those godly people
p: Blood here is life given. The Bible's sacrifices worked through blood, and so does this martyr death.
b: In the law of Moses "It is the blood that makes atonement, by means of the life in it" (Leviticus 17:11). The speaker speaks of the martyrs' blood in the same way: through their blood God saved Israel. The New Testament says that Christians are made right with God "by his blood" (Romans 3:25; 5:9) and that "no forgiveness comes about without blood being poured out" (Hebrews 9:22). In the law the blood is an animal's; in 4 Maccabees it is human martyrs'; in the New Testament it is Christ's.

a: atoning
p: The word Paul uses for Christ in Romans 3:25. Here it is an adjective; Sinaiticus makes it a noun.
b: Hilasterios comes from the verb hilaskomai, "to make atonement, to appease". As a noun, hilasterion, it is the Greek Old Testament's word for the atonement lid of the ark, where blood was sprinkled on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:14-15; Hebrews 9:5), and in Greek religion a gift dedicated to appease a god. English versions here say "propitiatory" (turning away God's anger: Brenton) or "atoning"; some scholars prefer "expiatory" (removing sin). The Plain English Translation says "atoning", which covers both. Paul calls Christ the hilasterion in Romans 3:25 ("the place of atonement"). See the variant and the chapter page.
orig: ἱλαστηρίου (hilasteriou)

a: divine providence saved Israel
t: Compared with the Bible: martyrs who save
p: The book says God saved Israel through the martyrs' deaths. Christians say only Christ's death atones.
b: Agrees in pattern, conflicts in claim for most Christians. The pattern of one who suffers for others is in Isaiah 53: "He bore the sin of many, and he will step in for the rebels" (Isaiah 53:12). 4 Maccabees applies it to the martyrs: their death was the turning point, and God then gave Judas his victories (18:4). The New Testament applies the pattern to Christ alone: "With one offering he has made perfect, for all time, the people who are being made holy" (Hebrews 10:14). Whether the sufferings of faithful people can share in atoning for others is asked on the card at 2 Maccabees 7:37-38; the churches' answers are there. See also 6:28-29.

a: he held up their endurance to his soldiers as an example
p: No other source says Antiochus praised the martyrs to his army. Townshend doubted it.
b: Only 4 Maccabees tells this. Townshend (1913) wrote that "one would like further evidence". He also noted that Antiochus did campaign in the east after the persecution, but that the speaker leaves out his failure: 1 Maccabees tells how he tried to plunder a temple city in Elymais in Persia, "But he could not" (1 Maccabees 6:3), and soon died. The speaker uses the story as a moral: even the tyrant had to admit their endurance. The punishment of Antiochus follows a few verses later (18:5).

a: Israelites, children born of Abraham's line
p: At the end the speaker speaks straight to his hearers as Abraham's children and asks them to obey the law.
b: The speech turns from praise to appeal. The hearers are "Israelites" and "children of Abraham's seed", the same family as the martyrs (18:23). "This law" is the law of Moses the martyrs died for. Townshend (1913) reports that some scholars thought the speech once ended at 18:2, with the thesis proved; he argued that the closing verses belong to it (see the chapter page).
orig: Ὦ τῶν Ἀβραμιαίων σπερμάτων ἀπόγονοι παῖδες Ἰσραηλεῖται (O ton Abramiaion spermaton apogonoi paides Israeleitai)

a: not only of the pains that come from within but also of those that come from outside
p: Inner pains are grief and fear; outer pains are wounds. Reason rules both.
b: Townshend (1913) explains: the pains "from within" are mental sufferings, such as the mother's grief and the brothers' love for each other; the pains "from outside" are bodily, the tortures. The book has shown both: Eleazar and the sons mastered the pain of the body, the mother the pain of the heart.

a: a share from God
p: Meris, a 'portion' or 'share', like a share of an inheritance.
b: Theias meridos, "a divine portion". The word is used for a share of land or inheritance. The Psalms call God himself the believer's share: "The LORD is the share I was given, and my cup" (Psalm 16:5). Paul gives thanks that God "has made you fit to share in the lot of the saints in the light" (Colossians 1:12). Here the martyrs' share is life with God after death (17:18; 18:23).
orig: θείας μερίδος κατηξιώθησαν (theias meridos katexiothesan)

a: drove the enemy out by siege
p: The book passes over the war of Judas in one line: the martyrs' death came first, then peace.
b: 1 and 2 Maccabees tell of years of fighting by Judas Maccabeus and his brothers, the cleansing of the temple in 164 BC (1 Maccabees 4:36-59) and the restoring of the law. 4 Maccabees sums it all up in one verse and credits the result to the martyrs: "through them". 2 Maccabees makes the same link: after the martyrs, as Judas gathered his men, "the Lord's anger had now turned to mercy" (2 Maccabees 8:5). The Greek is awkward: "the nation" (to ethnos) is neuter, but the participle "having renewed" is masculine singular. Townshend (1913) says that if this reading is kept, a masculine word such as "Israel" must be understood as the subject. Sinaiticus and Venetus have plural forms, which make the subject "they", and the first hand of Sinaiticus and Venetus also have a different verb, "they have sacked" (see the variant). Townshend judged the statement historically correct.

a: now that he is dead he is still being punished
t: Compared with the Bible: punished after death
p: The tyrant suffers on earth and after death. 2 Maccabees tells his painful death; 4 Maccabees adds his torment after it.
b: Goes beyond. 2 Maccabees 9 tells how Antiochus died in agony, struck by God. 4 Maccabees says he is punished still, after death, as the brothers warned him (9:9; 12:12; 18:22). The Hebrew Bible says little about punishment after death (Isaiah 66:24; Daniel 12:2). The New Testament teaches judgment after death (Hebrews 9:27; Luke 16:23-24). Antiochus's fate is the dark mirror of the martyrs': they live with God, he is tormented.
orig: ἀποθανὼν κολάζεται (apothanon kolazetai)

a: took his army against the Persians
p: 1 Maccabees says Antiochus went to Persia for money. 4 Maccabees makes it a retreat from failure.
b: 1 Maccabees says Antiochus decided "to go to Persia, to collect the tribute of those lands and raise a great deal of money" (1 Maccabees 3:31). His campaign in the east ended with his death (1 Maccabees 6:1-16). 4 Maccabees makes his departure the result of his failure in Jerusalem. Brenton (1851) puts the words that introduce the mother's speech at the start of his 18:7, not at the end of 18:6.

a: I guarded the rib that was built
p: She means her own body, a woman's body, which Genesis says God 'built' from Adam's rib.
b: The words come from the Greek of Genesis 2:22, which says God "built" (okodomesen) the rib into a woman: "The LORD God built the rib he had taken from the man into a woman" (Genesis 2:22). So "the built rib" is the woman's body. (Here Swete prints Venetus's "that was built"; Alexandrinus and Sinaiticus have "that was being built", see the variant.) The mother says she kept it pure. Townshend (1913) added "into Eve" in his translation to make the sense clear, and reports that the scholar Grimm had once read it as "the woman's side of the house" before giving that up. She did not leave her father's house: in that world, a sign of a carefully guarded daughter.
orig: ἐφύλασσον δὲ τὴν ᾠκοδομημένην πλευράν (ephylasson de ten okodomemenen pleuran)

a: No destroyer of the wilderness, no seducer in the open field, ruined me.
p: The law spoke of a girl attacked in the open field; and the snake deceived Eve.
b: The law of Moses deals with a girl attacked "out in the open country", where no one heard her cry (Deuteronomy 22:25-27). Townshend (1913) read "the destroyer of the wilderness" as a desert demon, from the belief that evil spirits haunted the waste places. The "destroyer who deceives, the snake" is the snake of Eden: "The snake fooled me, and I ate" (Genesis 3:13). Paul fears that "just as the snake fooled Eve with his cunning" the Corinthians may be led astray (2 Corinthians 11:3). Unlike Eve, the mother was not deceived.

a: When these children were grown
p: 'These' has nothing before it to point to. Townshend thought words were lost.
b: The Greek says "when these had come of age", but the speech has not yet named her sons. Townshend (1913) suggested that words such as "and bore him seven sons" were lost between 18:8 and 18:9. Another explanation is that she points to her sons standing before her. The Plain English Translation says "these children" to keep the Greek's pointing word.
orig: τούτων δὲ ἐνηλίκων γενομένων ἐτελεύτησεν ὁ πατήρ (touton de enelikon genomenon eteleutesen ho pater)

a: the law and the prophets
p: The father did what Deuteronomy asks: he taught his children the law at home.
b: "The law and the prophets" is a name for the Scriptures, used by Jesus: "That is the Law and the Prophets" (Matthew 7:12). Deuteronomy tells parents to teach God's words: "Repeat them to your children again and again" (Deuteronomy 6:7). The list that follows (18:11-19) shows what such teaching held: stories of righteous sufferers and words of hope. The mother's speech is the only place in the book where we see the family at home before the persecution.

a: Abel, killed by Cain
p: The list begins with Abel, the first person killed for doing right, as Jesus' list does.
b: The father's reading begins with Abel, killed by his brother (Genesis 4:8). Jesus also begins with him: "from the blood of Abel the righteous to the blood of Zechariah" (Matthew 23:35). Hebrews says that through his sacrifice Abel "still speaks, though he died" (Hebrews 11:4). Such lists of heroes were a Jewish way of teaching (Sirach 44-50; 1 Maccabees 2:51-60; Hebrews 11). This one is chosen for the sons: nearly every name is someone who suffered or faced death for God.
r: Genesis 4:8; Matthew 23:35; Hebrews 11:4; Hebrews 12:24; Sirach 44:1-50:24; 1 Maccabees 2:51-60

a: Isaac, offered as a whole burnt offering
p: The Greek calls Isaac 'wholly offered', the word of Genesis 22:2 in Greek, as though the sacrifice were done.
b: Holokarpoumenon means "offered whole as a burnt offering". The Greek of Genesis 22:2 uses the noun from the same root (holokarposis) for what God asked. Isaac was not killed, but the father speaks of him as an offering made. Hebrews says Abraham "offered Isaac" and, "in a kind of parable", got him back from the dead (Hebrews 11:17-19). See 13:12 and 16:20.
orig: τὸν ὁλοκαρπούμενον Ἰσαάκ (ton holokarpoumenon Isaak)

a: Joseph in prison
p: Joseph suffered unjustly in prison before God raised him up.
b: Joseph was thrown into prison on a false charge: "he stayed, in the prison house" (Genesis 39:20). He kept faith there and was raised to rule Egypt. The book used Joseph earlier as a model of self-control (2:2-3). Here he is a righteous sufferer whom God did not forget.

a: Phinehas the zealous one
p: Phinehas killed an Israelite and a Midianite woman to stop a plague. He became the model of zeal for the law.
b: Phinehas "has turned my rage back from the Israelites. He was zealous with my zeal" (Numbers 25:11). He stopped a plague by killing the sinners, and "It was reckoned to him as righteousness" (Psalm 106:31). 1 Maccabees makes him the model of Mattathias, who "was zealous for the law, as Phinehas had been" (1 Maccabees 2:26). Phinehas is the only one in the list who suffered nothing; he is there for his zeal, and because his act turned God's anger from Israel. Sirach says of him, "he made atonement for Israel" (Sirach 45:23), as the martyrs' deaths do here (17:22).
r: Numbers 25:6-13; Numbers 25:11; Psalm 106:30-31; 1 Maccabees 2:26; 1 Maccabees 2:54; Sirach 45:23-24

a: Daniel in the lions' pit
p: Daniel was thrown to the lions and shut in a pit, and God shut the lions' mouths.
b: The Greek lakkos is a pit or cistern, the word the Greek of Daniel 6 uses for the lions' den. Daniel said, "My God sent his angel to shut the lions' mouths" (Daniel 6:22). The father "called him blessed", the word for one God has favored. Daniel and the three (18:12) are the heroes the book uses most (13:9; 16:3, 21).
orig: τὸν ἐν λάκκῳ λεόντων Δανιήλ (ton en lakko leonton Daniel)

a: Even if you walk through fire, the flame will not burn you.
p: From Isaiah 43:2, in the words of its Greek, which fit the three in the furnace.
b: The words are Isaiah 43:2 in Greek, shortened: kan dia pyros dielthes, phlox ou katakausei se. The Plain English Translation of the Hebrew reads: "If you walk in the fire, you will not get burned, / and the flame will not catch you" (Isaiah 43:2). The promise was first for exiles going home. Here it is applied to martyrs, and the sons will be burned. The father taught the promise as faith that God is with his people in the fire, even when he does not stop it.
orig: Κἂν διὰ πυρὸς διέλθῃς, φλὸξ οὐ κατακαύσει σε (Kan dia pyros dielthes, phlox ou katakausei se)

a: Many are the troubles of the righteous.
p: The quotation stops before the psalm's promise of rescue.
b: The words are Psalm 34:19 (33:20 in the Greek numbering): pollai hai thlipseis ton dikaion. The Plain English Translation of the Hebrew reads: "Many are the evils that strike a righteous person, / but out of all of them the LORD rescues him" (Psalm 34:19). The speech quotes only the first half. For sons about to die, the troubles are certain; the rescue will come after death. John 19:36 applies the next verse of the psalm to Jesus.
orig: Πολλαὶ αἱ θλίψεις τῶν δικαίων (Pollai hai thlipseis ton dikaion)

a: It is a tree of life to all who do his will.
p: Proverbs 3:18 says wisdom is a tree of life to those who hold her. This form speaks of doing his will.
b: Proverbs 3:18 reads in the Plain English Translation: "To those who grab hold of her she is a tree of life". The Greek of Proverbs (Swete) says much the same: a tree of life "to all who hold fast to her". The form here is different: "to all who do his will". It may be a quotation from memory or another form of the text; it turns wisdom into obedience to God, which is how the book understands wisdom (1:15-17). The tree of life goes back to Eden (Genesis 2:9) and forward to the new Jerusalem (Revelation 22:2).
orig: Ξύλον ζωῆς ἐστιν πᾶσιν τοῖς ποιοῦσιν αὐτοῦ τὸ θέλημα (Xylon zoes estin pasin tois poiousin autou to thelema)

a: Will these dry bones live?
p: The one resurrection text in a book that never speaks of resurrection.
b: Ezekiel was asked in his vision, "will these bones live?" (Ezekiel 37:3); the quotation adds "dry" from Ezekiel 37:4. In Ezekiel the bones are Israel, dead in exile, and God raises them as a nation. Jews and Christians later read the vision as a promise of the resurrection of the dead. It is striking here: elsewhere 4 Maccabees speaks only of immortal souls, never of bodies raised (see the chapter page). The place of 18:6-19 in the book is debated (see the chapter page), and this verse is worth weighing in that debate: either the speaker used a familiar text of hope without pressing its sense, or these verses carry a different hope from the rest of the speech.
orig: Εἰ ζήσεται τὰ ὀστᾶ τὰ ξηρὰ ταῦτα (Ei zesetai ta osta ta xera tauta)

a: I will kill, and I will make alive.
p: Deuteronomy 32:39: the God who kills is the God who gives life. Here both verbs are future.
b: The Song of Moses says: "I kill, and I make alive; / I strike down, and I make well" (Deuteronomy 32:39). Here both Greek verbs are future, apokteno kai zen poieso, so the Plain English Translation says "I will kill, and I will make alive". The Greek of Deuteronomy 32:39 (Swete) has a present, apoktenno, "I kill", and the same future, zen poieso. Hannah's song says the same (1 Samuel 2:6). In 2 Maccabees the brothers quote the same song, from Deuteronomy 32:36 (2 Maccabees 7:6). For the sons, the verse means that death by the king's order is not the end, because life and death belong to God.
orig: Ἐγὼ ἀποκτενῶ, καὶ ζῇν ποιήσω (Ego apokteno, kai zen poieso)

a: This is your life
p: From Deuteronomy 30:20: loving God and holding to him is life itself.
b: Moses ended his call to choose life with these words: "He is your life, and he gives you long days to live on the land" (Deuteronomy 30:20). The Greek of that verse says: "this is your life and the length of your days". In Deuteronomy the long days are life in the land. In the mother's mouth, "life" means life with God that death cannot end. On "happiness" or "length", see the variant.
orig: Αὕτη ἡ ζωὴ ὑμῶν (Haute he zoe hymon)

a: O bitter day, and yet not bitter
p: The speaker says 'bitter' three times: a bitter day, yet not bitter, under a bitter tyrant.
b: The repetition of pikros, "bitter", is a speaker's device. The day was bitter for the family's suffering and not bitter because of its outcome. The tyrant is "of the Greeks", a rare plain naming of the enemy as Greek in a speech that uses Greek learning everywhere. The "catapult" (katapeltes) is the torture frame of 8:13 and the brothers' deaths, not a weapon.
orig: Ὦ πικρᾶς τῆς τότε ἡμέρας, καὶ οὐ πικρᾶς (O pikras tes tote hemeras, kai ou pikras)

a: divine Justice
p: Dike, Justice, is pictured as a person who goes after the guilty.
b: He theia dike, "divine Justice". Here Justice is pictured as a person who goes after the wrongdoer. The book uses the figure for God's justice (see 4:21; 8:14, 22; 9:9; 12:12). Acts has the islanders of Malta say of Paul, "Justice won't let him go on living" (Acts 28:4). The tyrant is called alastor, a word for a man under a curse and for an avenging spirit: "the accursed man".
orig: ἡ θεία δίκη μετῆλθεν καὶ μετελεύσεται τὸν ἀλάστορα (he theia dike metelthen kai meteleusetai ton alastora)

a: are gathered together
p: As Abraham and Jacob were 'gathered to their people', the martyrs are gathered to their fathers.
b: Genesis says: "Abraham breathed his last and died at a good old age, old and satisfied, and he was gathered to his people" (Genesis 25:8), and the same of Jacob (Genesis 49:33). The speech ends with the martyrs and their mother gathered "in the place of their fathers". The Greek verb synagelazontai means "are herded together", as a flock is gathered. The welcome the brothers hoped for in 13:17 has happened.
orig: εἰς πατέρων χῶρον συναγελάζονται (eis pateron choron synagelazontai)

a: From God they have received souls that are pure
t: Compared with the Bible: pure and immortal souls
p: The book ends with immortal souls, not raised bodies. 2 Maccabees and the New Testament hope for resurrection.
b: Differs. The book's last picture is of souls, "pure and immortal", received from God. The verb apeilephotes can mean "received back" or "received as their due". Townshend (1913) thought the words suggest that souls existed before birth, comparing the Wisdom of Solomon: "a good soul was given me as my share" (Wisdom of Solomon 8:19). In 2 Maccabees the same martyrs hope that God "will raise us" bodily (2 Maccabees 7:9). The New Testament hopes for both: to be with Christ after death (Philippians 1:23) and the raising of the body (1 Corinthians 15:42-44). Whether the soul is immortal by nature is asked on the card at Wisdom of Solomon 3.
orig: ψυχὰς ἁγνὰς καὶ ἀθανάτους ἀπειληφότες παρὰ τοῦ θεοῦ (psychas hagnas kai athanatous apeilephotes para tou theou)
r: Wisdom of Solomon 3:1-4; Wisdom of Solomon 8:19-20; 2 Maccabees 7:9; 2 Maccabees 7:14; Philippians 1:23; 1 Corinthians 15:42-44; 14:5-6; 16:13

a: To him be the glory forever and ever. Amen.
p: The speech ends as a sermon does, with praise to God. Paul's letters use the same words.
b: The words ho he doxa eis tous aionas ton aionon, amen are the closing praise of Jewish and Christian prayer. Paul writes: "To him belongs the glory for ever and ever. Amen" (Galatians 1:5); "To him be the glory for all the ages. Amen" (Romans 11:36). The ending is one of the signs that this philosophical speech was meant for a gathering of worshipers. Venetus leaves out "of the ages".
orig: ᾧ ἡ δόξα εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. ἀμήν. (ho he doxa eis tous aionas ton aionon. amen.)
